http://arxiv.org/abs/2601.22807v1 | Ground Level Enhancement (GLE#77) in the gamma-ray component: First observation from Arctic and Antarctic stations | Pranali Thakur, Geeta Vichare, Selvaraj Chelliah | - | -
This article presents the observations of the extreme ground-level enhancement (GLE #77) of Solar Cycle 25 that occurred on 11 November 2025, using ground-based NaI(Tl) gamma-ray detectors deployed at Arctic and Antarctic stations, together with neutron monitor data and particle measurements from the GOES-18 satellite. The event was associated with an intense X-class solar flare and a strong solar energetic proton event. This paper reports the first ground-based detection of a GLE using gamma-ray detectors operating simultaneously in both polar regions, which are concurrent with increases in neutron monitor counts. Thus highlights the capability of polar gamma-ray detectors to complement traditional neutron monitor observations during extreme solar proton events. A detailed analysis revealed distinct prompt and delayed responses during the event evolution. Interestingly, the signature of the prompt peak of GLE#77 (at 10:38 UT) was observed up to high-rigidity neutron monitors (low latitudes). However, the delayed peak (at 13:08 UT) was not seen at the stations with rigidity > 6 GV. The timing of the prompt and delayed peaks coincided with the proton flux peaks observed by the GOES-18 satellite at energies > 150 MeV and 12-99 MeV, respectively. It is observed that the GLE amplitude has a strong dependence on geomagnetic cutoff rigidity and has a weak solar zenith angle dependence.

http://arxiv.org/abs/2601.02801v1 | Transient Large-Scale Anisotropy in TeV Cosmic Rays due to an Interplanetary Coronal Mass Ejection | Zhen Cao, F. Aharonian, Y. X. Bai, Y. W. Bao, D. Bastieri, X. J. Bi, Y. J. Bi, W. Bian, A. V. Bukevich, C. M. Cai, W. Y. Cao, Zhe Cao, J. Chang, J. F. Chang, A. M. Chen, E. S. Chen, G. H. Chen, H. X.  | Phys. Rev. Lett., 136, 251002 (2026) | 10.1103/mkk2-hbq5
Large- or medium-scale cosmic ray anisotropy at TeV energies has not previously been confirmed to vary with time. Transient anisotropy changes have been observed below 150 GeV, especially near the passage of an interplanetary shock and coronal mass ejection containing a magnetic flux rope ejected by a solar storm, which can trigger a geomagnetic storm with practical consequences. In such events, cosmic rays provide remote sensing of the magnetic field properties. Here we report the observation of transient large-scale anisotropy in TeV cosmic ray ions using data from the Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory (LHAASO). We analyze hourly skymaps of the transient cosmic ray intensity excess or deficit, the gradient of which indicates the direction and magnitude of transient large-scale anisotropy across the field of view. We observe enhanced anisotropy above typical hourly fluctuations with $>$5$σ$ significance during some hours of November 4, 2021, in separate data sets for four primary cosmic ray energy ranges of median energy from $E$=0.7 to 3.1 TeV. The gradient varies with energy as $E^γ$, where $γ\approx-0.5$. At a median energy $\leq$1.0 TeV, this gradient corresponds to a dipole anisotropy of at least 1\%, or possibly a weaker anisotropy of higher order. This new type of observation opens the opportunity to study interplanetary magnetic structures using air shower arrays around the world, complementing existing in situ and remote measurements of plasma properties.

http://arxiv.org/abs/2601.19289v1 | Continued activity of the 25th cycle: largest in 20 years. Ground-level enhancement and Forbush decrease | B. Sargsyan, A. Chilingarian | - | -
After a very calm 24th solar activity cycle, the 25th cycle has already seen several interesting events. A Ground Level Enhancement GLE77 was observed on 11 November 2025 following an X5.1 class solar flare. A strong Forbush decrease occurred on 19 and 20 January 2026 during one of the most intense geomagnetic storms of Solar Cycle 25. Events were recorded coherently by the global neutron monitor network and by SEVAN detectors at multiple altitudes. Using spectrometric capabilities, we reconstruct energy spectra of missing neutrons and muons during the FD and compare them with corresponding spectra measured during GLE77. The analysis demonstrates that FD and GLE signatures are intrinsically asymmetric. FDs selectively suppress the preexisting galactic cosmic ray population, whereas GLEs introduce an additional, harder particle component. Neutron and muon channels exhibit markedly different spectral behavior, particularly at higher deposited energies, reflecting their sensitivity to different primary energy ranges. These results show that combined NM and SEVAN observations provide robust, complementary diagnostics of rigidity dependent cosmic ray modulation during extreme heliospheric disturbances.

http://arxiv.org/abs/2605.10193v1 | Coronal Mass Ejection and Heliospheric Current Sheet Interaction Causing a Long-Duration Magnetic Field Sector Transition | Manuela Temmer, Stephan G. Heinemann, Nina Dresing, Mateja Dumbovic, Eleanna Asvestari | - | -
We present a study that combines remote-sensing and in-situ observations of coronal mass ejections (CMEs) interacting with the nearby heliospheric current sheet (HCS). The sequence of eruptive events under study culminates in the largest directly observed flare of solar cycle 25 on 3 October 2024, producing a fast halo CME. Their source region can be linked to a so-called nested active region (or active longitude) that persisted over several solar rotations. Such long-lived regions reflect deep-seated magnetic structures that shape the global magnetic field configuration. By applying the drag-based CME propagation model, we connect the near-Sun observations from several CMEs during that activity period with in-situ measurements. While one of the CMEs propagated on the opposite side of the HCS from Earth, and therefore did not produce in-situ signatures near Earth, we detect, over the period October 5-10, 2024, a complex of HCS and CME structures propagating together with a shock ahead of them. The HCS seems to be locally replaced by the CME signatures, leading to a long-duration sector reversal of more than 48 hours. This event highlights the intrinsic connection between solar surface structures, the global magnetic field, and the evolution of complex eruptive events.

Links: [{"title":"The 12 November 2025 Ugly Duckling Geomagnetic Storm: From the Sun to the Earth - PMC","url":"https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12986641/"},{"title":"ESA - Lessons from the November 2025 solar storm","url":"https://www.esa.int/Space_Safety/Space_weather/Lessons_from_the_November_2025_solar_storm"},{"title":"Unprecedented Multipoint Observation of Spatially Varying ICME Turbulence of Different Ages during October 2024 Extreme Solar Storm at 1 AU","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.13644"},{"title":"Multi-instrument constraints on a hemispherically asymmetric positive ionospheric storm in the 60-180 deg E sector during the 12-13 November 2025 geomagnetic storm","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.14454"},{"title":"NOAA Shares First Space Weather Data from SWFO-L1’s Magnetometer","url":"https://www.nesdis.noaa.gov/news/noaa-shares-first-space-weather-data-swfo-l1s-magnetometer"},{"title":"Quasi-planar ICME sheath: a cause of first two-step extreme geomagnetic storm of 25th solar cycle observed on 23 April 2023","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2305.05381"},{"title":"An Intense Geomagnetic Storm Originated from Stealth Coronal Mass Ejection: Remote and In Situ Observations by Near Radially Aligned Spacecraft - IOPscience","url":"https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.3847/1538-4357/ae0992"},{"title":"Ionospheric Mechanisms Leading to Plasma‐Bubble Zonal Drift Reversal and Deformation During the 12 November 2025 Geomagnetic Storm - Picanço - 2026 - Space Weather - Wiley Online Library","url":"https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2026SW005063?af=R"},{"title":"Influence of ICME-driven Magnetic Cloud-like and Sheath Region induced Geomagnetic Storms in causing anomalous responses of the Low-latitude Ionosphere: A Case Study","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.14659"}]

The search turned up several papers on the 11–12 November 2025 storm, though none is clearly the Space Weather paper with the exact title you described.

- **Ionospheric paper in Space Weather (2026):** A Wiley/AGU paper on plasma-bubble drift during the 12 November 2025 storm appears in *Space Weather* in 2026. It describes the pre-storm quiet interval and the storm onset near 00:10 UT on 12 November, which it links to successive ICME impacts. The interplanetary conditions during the early and peak storm main phase are consistent with forcing by successive ICME impacts.
- **Solar-wind and ICME structure:** A PMC article titled "The 12 November 2025 Ugly Duckling Geomagnetic Storm" says the storm was triggered by a complex shock-ICME structure as a result of three ICMEs and driven shocks that arrived on 11–12 November. Its main field enhancement sat in the sheath behind the shock from the second ICME. The snippet doesn't name the journal, so I can't confirm it's the one you're after.
- **Solar-wind speed jump:** An arXiv paper on ionospheric effects reports that solar wind speed rose sharply from about 400 km/s to roughly 750–850 km/s during the event.
- **L1 observations:** NOAA reports first magnetometer data from SWFO-L1, taken about 40 minutes before the CME began affecting Earth's environment.
- **Timing:** ESA reports the CME reached Earth at 18:50 UTC on 12 November, and that the storm peaked for about six hours.

Next steps: the PMC paper is the most likely candidate for the ICME/L1 analysis. Its journal and DOI should be checked directly, and the *Space Weather* ionospheric paper (DOI 10.1029/2026SW005063) is the best match for the AGU 2026 requirement.

The search turned up good detail on the CME's launch and Earth arrival, but nothing on STEREO-A in situ data, PLASTIC, or the Solar Orbiter, BepiColombo, or Mars observations.

- **Eruption and CME:** A large halo CME was first seen by STEREO A COR2 at 2025-11-11T10:23Z. It was tied to an X5.1 flare from Active Region 14274 (N27W27) which peaked at 2025-11-11T10:04Z.
- **Kinematics:** One CCMC analysis gives a radial speed of 1856.0 km/s and a half angle of 45 deg.
- **Earth arrival:** The arrival was likely observed at L1 by ACE/DSCOVR around 2025-11-12T18:52Z, with Btotal increasing from 19nT to about 40nT by 19:00Z. An earlier scoreboard prediction had shock arrival at 2025-11-13 04:20 with a predicted transit time of 41.95 hours.
- **Model updates:** A later ensemble WSA-ENLIL + Cone update was issued on 2025-11-12, which is labeled a beta product, and the ensemble product is still in development mode.
- **Other missions:** A DONKI notification lists Juno, BepiColombo, OSIRIS-APEX, Solar Orbiter, STEREO A, Missions Near Earth as message recipients. That is a distribution list, not evidence of detection at those spacecraft.
- **Gaps:** I found no STEREO-A in situ arrival time or PLASTIC plasma measurements, and no confirmed Solar Orbiter, BepiColombo, or Mars in situ observations. Those would need a targeted follow-up search, such as the STEREO science team or the PLASTIC instrument papers.

The search didn't turn up anything about 3I/ATLAS. None of the results mention the comet, its location, or any simulation of it. The results are general WSA-ENLIL+Cone material from the CCMC, so they can't answer whether a 3I/ATLAS simulation exists in DONKI.

What the results do cover:

- **What DONKI holds:** The CCMC's DONKI database includes WSA-ENLIL+Cone CME simulations, ICME arrivals, high speed streams and related space weather records.
- **Typical record layout:** DONKI WSA-ENLIL pages list model inputs, then an Earth impact section and an "Other Location(s) Impact" section for spacecraft and planets. Examples include a glancing blow at Earth with a Kp range and little or no impact to Earth.
- **Model basis:** The simulations are driven by CME parameters from coronagraph observations, as described in measurements derived from coronagraphs.

These records are built around solar CMEs. A comet would not normally be a WSA-ENLIL input, so a 3I/ATLAS record is unlikely to exist in that form. If you need its location or any impact modeling, search the CCMC DONKI site directly or check NASA's comet-tracking pages.

The search didn't turn up a paper that models solar wind speed or density at 3I/ATLAS's perihelion, or one that covers the hydrogen coma and charge-exchange ionization together. The closest hits are observational and modeling work on the coma and water production:

- **SOHO/SWAN water production (ApJ Letters, Feb 2026):** A Monte Carlo study of the hydrogen coma from SWAN Lyman-α maps, covering November to December 2025 at roughly 1.4 to 2.2 au. It reports a peak post-perihelion water production rate near 4×10^28 s^-1 ([1-4, 1-5]). A separate ApJ Letter from the same SWAN data reports 3.17×10^29 s^-1 on November 6, at 1.40 au ([5-3]).
- **Perihelion asymmetry (arXiv 2601.15443):** The same SWAN dataset, analyzed with a particle trajectory model ([2-3, 2-11]).
- **Pre-perihelion volatiles (arXiv 2602.14218):** Argues that extended coma sources contribute heavily to water measurements before perihelion, up to about 80% from 3 to 2 au ([6-2]).
- **X-ray detection:** ESA's XMM-Newton observed X-ray emission from gas colliding with the solar wind, a process tied to charge exchange. The source is a project tracker page, not a peer-reviewed paper ([8-3, 8-4]).
- **Plasma tail:** Juice's Janus camera imaged an ion tail and plasma interactions that altered its structure ([9-4, 9-5]).

For solar wind speed and density specifically, the results don't contain a direct model. A follow-up search on the XMM-Newton X-ray paper or on "3I/ATLAS ion tail plasma model" would be the most likely route to one.

The search didn't turn up an SWPC product confirming a G3 storm on 3 December 2025. The closest match is from Australia's space weather centre, which reported that the Earth entered a coronal hole wind stream in the second half of the UT day on 03-Dec. That same warning said planetary activity hit G3 for one period, between 18:00 and 21:00 UT on 3 December, and was still at G1 when issued.

The SWPC forecast discussion issued at 00:30 UTC on 3 December matches the driver but not the level. It expected disturbances in the solar wind from a recurrent, equatorial, negative-polarity coronal hole high-speed stream, with enhanced field ahead of the fast wind (a CIR). Its rationale called for G2 levels on 3–4 December, citing a combination of activity from a CIR/CH HSS and the arrival of a glancing blow from the 01 Dec CME.

Separately, SWPC's G3 watch for 9 December was for a different event: a full-halo coronal mass ejection (CME), associated with an M8.1 flare from Region 4299, which was expected to arrive early to midday on 9 December.

I did not find the SWPC product that actually reported the 3 December observations, so the G3 level rests on the Australian source. Searching for SWPC's 4 December daily report or its event summary would confirm it.
